HEADLINE: APRA's pay commandments closer
TEXT:
APRA's remake of banker pay will have ramifications for other sectors of the economy.

The end-of-year annual general meeting season for three of our big banks was always going to be tense, given Westpac, ANZ and NAB all face second strikes (25 per cent negative votes) against their remuneration report.

But the prudential regulator is likely to add a new level of drama when it releases its long-awaited update to executive pay standards some time in the next six weeks.

While the banks are hard at work tweaking their own pay models to avoid a second strike, the smoke signals emanating from the other side of the fence suggest the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority's early guidance on the standards - delivered by chairman Wayne Byres at The Australian Financial Review Banking & Wealth Summit in April - was no thought bubble. Byres said in April he was taking the Hayne royal commission's recommendation for a cap on the level of financial metrics used to decide long-term incentives seriously. Similarly, it is understood Byres was not just jawboning when he said a 50 per cent split between financial and non-financial incentives was a good place to start. Exactly where the cap on financial metrics eventually sits remains to be seen and there will be an inevitable consultation period. But it looks very much like the cap is coming.

The tilt towards non-financial metrics won't please many investors and proxy advisers. While it's true that many don't like these metrics, that's not necessarily the big concern.

Rather, investors and advisers worry that basing long-term incentives on metrics around risk, culture, strategy, customer service and staff will put too much discretion into the hands of boards that have not earned investor trust in recent years. This is particularly the case where boards have rubber-stamped fat bonus numbers spat out by a balanced scorecard during periods where the banks have battled scandals. APRA's more prescriptive pay standards will clearly make life difficult for the chairs of remuneration committees who are toiling to design pay schemes that can broadly satisfy everyone - perhaps more realistically, find a level of dissatisfaction that all sides can accept, given how imperfect pay structures are.

But there is also an argument that APRA's push on non-financial metrics could make life easier for boards who want to head in this direction. Remember, the Commonwealth Bank board was handed a strike in 2016 after trying to link pay more closely to non-financial metrics, after investors protested the loosening of ties between pay and shareholder returns.

A final point worth making is that APRA's pronouncements in the financial sector will have clear ramifications for the rest of the market. Surely non-financial risks will play a much important role in the pay structures of all sectors.

Our growth stocks are the

world's most expensive

Australian fund managers are having one of their worst runs in the past 15 years. But the reason for their underperformance might eventually turn out to be good news - they are shunning local growth stocks, which are the most overvalued in the world.

That's the central conclusion from a fascinating examination of Australia's hottest stocks, led by Goldman Sachs' head of portfolio strategy and quantitative research, Matthew Ross.

To understand the rise and rise of Australia's growth stocks - defined as companies worth more than $500 million forecast to deliver earnings-per-share growth of more than 20 per cent over the next two years - and how they have performed relative to global growth stocks, Ross and his colleagues Bill Zu and Hannah Layman looked at every stock that fitted the above criteria across the world's 13 largest equity markets.

The team excluded stocks with large expected earnings from cyclical sectors - mining, energy, banks, transport, engineering and construction - to isolate what they see as true growth firms. They found 22 per cent of stocks across major equity markets fell into the high-growth bucket.

The list in Australia includes much-hyped companies including WiseTech, Afterpay, Altium, Xero and Appen - the so-called WAAXA stocks - but also household names such as News Corp, Breville, A2 Milk and Bellamy's, Blackmores, Seek, Cochlear, CSL, REA Group and Domain.

The comparison between Australia and other big markets is stunning. High growth stocks in Australia now trade on a median forward price-to-earnings multiple of 39.8 times, having delivered an average share price return of 62 per cent over the past 12 months.

This compares with a global average of a multiple of 23.5 times. Australia's median is also a full 25 per cent higher than the US, which is the second most expensive market for growth stocks, with an average P/E of 31.5 times.

Ross and his team then went on to examine some of the reasons for this big Australian premium.

Could it be low interest rates creating an overexcited chase for yield?

Probably not. Australia's 10-year bond yields are still relatively high on a global basis (below only China and the US) and even in markets where interest rates are negative, growth stocks attract a much lower premium in Australia.

Could it be scarcity? The idea that high-growth stocks are rare in a market such as Australia that is both relatively small and dominated by banks and miners? High-growth stocks do make up 11 per cent of the local market by number and just 3 per cent by market cap, after all.

But growth stocks are similarly scarce but much less expensive in France (where high-growth stocks are 1 per cent of all stocks by market cap but on a P/E multiple of 17.7 times), Switzerland (2 per cent of market cap, multiple 27.1 times), Germany (4 per cent of market cap, multiple of 31.1 times) and Canada (5 per cent of market cap, 25.3 times).

Not surprisingly, large institutional investors appear to be increasingly wary of buying into Australia's shooting stars. Some of the evidence is anecdotal.

Dion Hershan, managing director and head of Australian equities at Yarra Capital Management - who told clients this week that in "a market which is probably over-heating, the top quintile of stocks by valuation looks like a furnace" - is one of many bemused fundies who will tell you things have become silly.

But there's hard data too. Ross says surveys of fund manager returns also suggest "the median manager is currently suffering one of the worst stretches of relative performance over the past 15 years", with returns trailing the benchmark by 390 basis points.

Lagging the market is never fun, but it might be no bad thing if we see the correction that many, including Hershan, expect.

The Goldman Sachs research says that although growth firms have outperformed the ASX 200 by 2.1 per cent over the past 20 years, the subset of high-growth firms that display warning signs of poor performance - which he says includes weak share price momentum, large share issuance, high gearing, large goodwill balances, lower profitability and very stretched valuations - have underperformed the market by an average of 15.5 per cent a year.

The growth companies that score highest on the warning-sign scale include infrastructure player Qube, telecommunications takeover target Vocus, vitamins group Blackmores, News Corporation, dairy group Bellamy's, payments group Afterpay Touch, Domain, Cleanaway Waste, Seek, funerals group Invocare and financial services groups IRESS and Hub24.

j.thomson@afr.com

Andrew Forrest's many entanglements with Buru Energy's Eric Streitberg

Fortescue founder Andrew "Twiggy" Forrest has, since 2016, been pursuing a PhD in marine ecology. But we wonder if it's not just ecological expertise he's been picking up in his studies.

Last week Street Talk revealed that the Rich Lister had been creeping up the register of gas junior Buru Energy, his holdings confirmed a few days later at 4.2 per cent of the company. Street Talk reported that the billionaire was particularly attracted to Buru's petroleum assets.

Buru's executive chairman is Eric Streitberg, whose partner is leading marine biologist Jessica Meeuwig.

That's a name Forrest should know, and not just because of putting his money into Streitberg's company. Forrest's PhD is being completed at the Centre for Marine Futures, at which Meeuwig is the inaugural director. It's a small institute, and Meeuwig has been a co-author of all four of the academic publications listed on Forrest's PhD profile.

So, did Twiggy Forest spot an investment idea from his PhD in saving the oceans? Wouldn't put it past him!

But he has other links to Buru as well: the investment was made through his private company Squadron Energy, which through a joint venture is exploring in tenements adjacent to those Buru is already producing from in the Canning Basin.

It's a small world.

Curtains for Vanda Gould's $383m tax panto

It will come as a shock to readers to learn that the Anglican church's favourite accountant, Vanda Gould, has been defrocked, over the trifling matter of a $383 million tax fraud.

Yes, it seems way harsh, but the Tax Practitioners Board is firm: no more tax returns from Vanda, merely because of some findings of "sustained, calculated and layered dishonesty" made by Justice Nye Perram.

Actually Perram said a bit more in his 2014 Hua Wang Bank judgment about Gould's offshore operations. He slipped in the phrase "crooked pantomime". Oh yes.

And he directed his findings be forwarded to ASIC, the Director of Public Prosecutions and the Australian Federal Police to consider "disgraceful" conduct, money laundering, tax fraud, and possibly insider trading.

That was almost five years ago. It's only now that the TPB has decided that Vanda has delighted Tax Office auditors long enough.

The TPB's new chief exec, Michael O'Neill, will be familiar with Gould's work because as assistant tax commissioner, O'Neill headed the mammoth Project Wickenby investigation. It was Wickenby's Operation Rubix that targeted Gould and clients, including former Sunland Group chairman John Leaver and colourful investor Joe Ross.

Gould, who donated millions to the Sydney Anglican church, had his clients send money to Hua Wang Bank in Samoa (which Gould secretly owned). The "bank" sent the money back as a loan to the clients, who claimed interest payments as a tax deduction, TPB affidavits said.

It was all a fine point of law, Gould's barrister John Hyde Page told the Administrative Appeals Tribunal last week, with the winsome appeal of a man who is never sure which end of a hobby horse he most resembles.

Yes, Hyde Page said of Gould, "he did control Hua Wang Bank, his clients did deposit money, Hua Wang Bank did make loans to his clients".

But TPB counsel Anthony McInerney SC "didn't explain why that's a bad thing", Hyde Page argued. "Tax planning is what people do."

And while tax assessments had totalled $383 million, settlements to date had raised only $63 million, with $21.9 million undisputed payments and three ongoing disputes for $18 million. This was hardly enough to take away the livelihood of a man who has been a tax agent for 40 years, was Hyde Page's gist.

AAT deputy president Ian Molloy was unconvinced and this week refused a stay on Gould's deregistration, citing Perram's findings of deceitful and dishonest conduct.

"The TPB is taking a firm approach to support honest taxpayers and their advisers by terminating those agents who fail their legal and ethical responsibilities," O'Neill said.

So far this year the TPB has deregistered 70 tax agents. New broom. Ouch.

For full disclosure, Gould once threatened to launch a private criminal prosecution of your (male) columnist. Now he's suing Tax Commissioner Chris Jordan for defamation. Why not?

Blue Sky directors put it behind them

With Blue Sky Alternative Investments in administration, the listed fund manager's directors are no longer in charge. And it seems board members past and present are keen to put the whole experience behind them.

Take John Kain, for seven years the company's chairman. In early 2018, the Adelaide corporate lawyer's eponymous firm used to note his chairmanship of Blue Sky as one of his "career highlights" on his biography, listing in some detail its growing assets under management and surging market capitalisation. By June the same year, this was reduced to a single sentence noting his chairmanship of the asset manager, and by September, it was gone entirely.

At least Kain still lists his role at Blue Sky on his LinkedIn profile. It's more than can be said for the very impressive independent directors appointed to the firm in late 2018. Many hold multiple ASX board positions dutifully listed in their online resumés. But their Blue Sky appointments don't appear to have made the cut.

Andrew Day acted as Blue Sky's executive chairman until the April 2019 appointment of a new CEO. But the most recent position on his LinkedIn is his CEO role at Hastings Fund Management that ended in 2017. John McDonald is another experienced fund manager, currently a non-executive director at Crestone (where he was previously executive chairman). Blue Sky isn't on his LinkedIn. Robert Kaye, who joined the board at the same time in December, certainly appears an active user of the service. But Blue Sky is, once again, missing. As for Cheryl Edwardes, the former WA Attorney- General, experienced ASX director and member of the Foreign Investment Review Board, she tendered her resignation from Blue Sky on May 21, the day after it went into receivership. Her five months at Blue Sky also aren't listed on LinkedIn.

In their defence, all joined well after Blue Sky's troubles began, and while presumably pocketing Blue Sky's director fees couldn't find a window in which to buy a single share between the lot of them. And who could blame them for that.

Meanwhile, Blue Sky's first meeting of creditors was over in roughly 30 minutes on Thursday. It was a quiet affair, our spies not seeing a single angry shareholder at Brisbane's Waterfront Place. Administrators Bradley Hellen and Nigel Markey of Pilot Partners say their investigations are continuing.

HEADLINE: Tech crowd rocket up Rich List
TEXT:
It took 16 years of the Rich List before the club of Australia's wealthiest 200 included a technology-sector tycoon. Back in 1998, Sean Howard, founder of OzEmail, was alone in a sea of property magnates and media moguls.

But tech has now arrived as a source of wealth creation in Australia. The Financial Review Rich List includes a record 14 technology entrepreneurs. They are led by Atlassian co-founders Scott Farquhar and Mike Cannon-Brookes who are in the top 10 for the first time, with fortunes of more than $9 billion each, after shares in their company nearly doubled in a year.

For the third year in a row, cardboard box king Anthony Pratt takes the No. 1 spot with estimated wealth of $15.57 billion, up from $12.90 billion. Iron ore miner Gina Rinehart is second (with wealth of $13.81 billion), followed by apartment mogul Harry Triguboff, who has defied the property slowdown to lift his wealth from $12.77 billion to $13.54 billion. Hong Kong-based property developer Hui Wing Mau is in fourth spot ($9.09 billion), followed by Farquhar and Cannon-Brookes.

This year's list includes a record 91 billionaires. Of the 200 entries, 129 are the founders of their businesses. Property remains the main vehicle by which fortunes are made, responsible for 63 entries, followed by retail, resources, investment and financial services. But those in tech, the sixth largest category, are easily the quickest builders of wealth.

The founder of global logistics software provider WiseTech, Richard White, rockets up 24 places to 20th with a $3.3 billion fortune, after materialising on the list in 2016.

The founders of buy-now-pay-later phenomenon Afterpay, zeitgeist fitness app Sweat, digital assets marketplace Envato, and medical imaging revolutioniser Pro Medicus have all barnstormed on to the list for the first time. Atlassian's Farquhar and Cannon-Brookes only entered the list in 2013, in lowly 190th and 191st place. Their team-collaboration software is now used by 138,000 organisations worldwide.

The theme of technology as a wealth accelerator could also be applied to the Bundaberg-based Greensill brothers of Greensill Capital, even though their official Rich List classification is financial services. Greensill's algorithmic ability to extract better supply-chain data and offer more attractive financing rates has been integral to it rapidly gaining nearly 1 million customers and a multibillion-dollar valuation.

Technology has also spawned a couple of blue-sky Rich Listers in Tim Kentley-Klay, co-founder of driverless car start-up Zoox, and Ori Allon, founder of luxury real estate brokerage Compass. Their valuations ballooned on big recent rounds of venture capital.

After Donald Trump slashed the corporate tax rate and granted instant write-offs for investment, Anthony Pratt grew pre-tax earnings 15 per cent to $1.26 billion. This put his family's valuation more than $1.5 billion clear of former list leaders Rinehart (No. 2) and Triguboff (No. 3).

Pratt's valuation was also fuelled by stronger price-to-earnings multiples for listed comparables like Amcor and Sonoco - not that his US-based Pratt Industries, or Australian cousin Visy, will be listed or sold while he has a say.

A minimum net worth of $472 million would get you on to the list in 2019. All valuations are ruled off in the first week of April. Some Rich Listers have since become much richer: the Greensills have doubled their valuation following an investment in May from Japan's Softbank. Meanwhile, the Atlassian founders would be ranked in second and third spot given the recent rally in the company's share price.

A change to the list's format in 2019 is the inclusion of families, which resulted in five new billionaire family entries: the daughters of Westfield co-founder John Saunders, the Buckeridges of BGC Construction fame, the Barro concrete kings, the Casella wine barons, and the Shahins of South Australian servo superiority.

The founders of these businesses have died, but the Rich List team decided that if their descendants still owned the business and were working together in it, these pools of wealth were too big to ignore.

This year the Rich List includes the valuations of the 50 people who almost made the list: many of them are old-timers who have been overtaken by newer Rich Listers, but there are some up-and-comers who seem destined to crack the Rich 200 in the near future. Notable inclusions are former Macquarie CEO Nicholas Moore (valued at $401 million), golfer Greg Norman ($355 million) and F45 founder Rob Deutsch ($315 million).

HEADLINE: Jack Ma: my life after Alibaba
TEXT:
Shanghai | Jack Ma, China's richest man and the founder of ecommerce giant Alibaba, has a message for the next generation of Financial Review Rich Listers - do not let celebrity go to your head.

"A lot of people want to stand in the centre of the stage, the spotlight on you. But that light has poison in it. Every move and the whole world looks at you," China's most scrutinised entrepreneur says in an exclusive interview with AFR Magazine.

"Social media makes entrepreneurs stars. Name, reputation brings you good stuff, but it also brings you bad stuff."

In a wide-ranging interview five months before he is due to step down as executive chairman of China's biggest technology company, Mr Ma, who is estimated to be worth $57 billion, credited Australia for inspiring his new mission to use his wealth to become a full-time philanthropist focusing on education and the environment.

Mr Ma's planned departure from the company he co-founded 20 years ago, which was announced last year, was a shock for investors. Alibaba is planning on a second listing in Hong Kong that could raise as much as $US20 billion to attract more funding from Asia as US-China trade tensions escalate, media reports said this week.

Mr Ma denied he was abandoning Alibaba at a time when a technology cold war was brewing between China and the United States, but said he would be around to help if his "child" got into trouble.

"I will never leave the company if it's a bad time. A lot of people work all their life in a company. If this company really wants to last ... we have to transition the company to the next generation and I have to do it while I'm young," the 54-year-old said.

Mr Ma is due to step down on September 10, 2019, passing the responsibility to current chief executive Daniel Zhang. Alibaba, which revolutionised the way China shops, also has a significant presence in Australia and facilitates the sale of billions of dollars worth of exports to China's middle classes via its Tmall platform.

Mr Ma, who rarely gives interviews, said he looked at setting up a fund focusing on environmental protection in Australia but was talked out of the idea because it was too difficult to get capital into the country. "I love Australia and I love going there. That's the country that changed my view of life," he said,

Mr Ma's special bond with Ken Morley, an electrical engineer from Newcastle in NSW, and his family, resulted in a $27 million scholarship program to the University of Newcastle two years ago. The Alibaba founder remains in contact with the late Mr Morley's children. "Friendship is what the relationship is built on and that's why it survived," said David Morley, a yoga teacher. "Dad would have been so proud of that."

Speaking with AFR Magazine at Alibaba's headquarters in Hangzhou, Mr Ma spoke for the first time about his personal challenges dealing with celebrity and the need to protect his privacy. "I understand that Jack Ma and Jack Me, they are different. Jack Ma has become the model image for a lot of people. But I'm not that guy," he said. "I don't want to take all the credit for Alibaba."

He revealed that he would devote 60 per cent of his time to his pet causes via his Jack Ma Foundation, with the remaining 40 per cent for "things that jump up, that are very interesting or I suddenly fall in love with". While Mr Ma is set to become the world's biggest high-profile philanthropist since Microsoft founder Bill Gates, he said he did not plan to sign up to the Giving Pledge, a Silicon Valley-led initiative where the world's super rich dedicate the majority of their wealth to charitable causes. Instead, he wants to manage his charitable pursuits himself and teach other billionaires to do the same.

"Spending money is more difficult than making money for me today," said Mr Ma, who topped the 2019 Hurun Rich List, which ranks China's wealthiest individuals. Forbes says he is China's second-wealthiest person with US$40 billion ($57 billion) after being eclipsed by another tech giant founder named Pony Ma.

"I did not expect I would be that wealthy and now I'm that wealthy, I have convinced myself that wealth is not mine."

Michael Smith's feature on Jack Ma is the cover story of the Rich List issue of AFR Magazine, inside today's Financial Review.

HEADLINE: New squeeze on big banks
TEXT:
The big four banks will face stronger competition from second-tier banks, which will be able to offer cheaper home loans and sharper deposit rates when the regulator moves to even the playing field for banks in the weeks ahead.

The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority is expected to reduce the relatively high-risk weighting applied to mortgages issued by smaller banks that determines how much capital they are required to hold to support their lending. That would narrow a key 10 percentage point regulatory advantage that allows the big banks to hold less capital.

The announcement is expected in the days following the Reserve Bank of Australia's meeting on Tuesday where financial markets have priced in a cash rate cut of 25 basis points to 1.25 per cent as a near certainty. It is hard on the heels of the prudential regulator's decision to remove a loan serviceability buffer that was unfairly penalising owner-occupiers.

The decision around risk weightings will be the first of three announcements to be rolled out by the prudential regulator over the next six weeks. The remaining two will concern loss absorbing capital buffers for big banks and a proposal to put a cap on financial incentives for executive pay.

The changes to risk weightings will shrink the gap between large and small banks and take any discussion about the weightings' impeding competition off the table.

The leg-up for smaller banks has occurred as speculation mounts of a merger between regional banks such as Bendigo and Adelaide Bank, Suncorp and Bank of Queensland.

Citi analyst Brendan Sproules said a spate of departures at the three banks since Monday, including Suncorp chief executive Michael Cameron, BoQ chairman Roger Davis and Bendigo Bank chairman Robert Johanson, heightened the potential for corporate activity. Mr Sproules said that with BoQ yet to announce a permanent successor to former chief executive Jon Sutton, who resigned for health reasons in December 2018, BoQ was "an obvious target in any potential consolidation talks".

Bank stocks were mixed yesterday, with ANZ down 0.2 per cent, Commonwealth Bank up 2 per cent, NAB up 0.3 per cent and Westpac down 0.7 per cent.

Smaller banks have long argued that the risk weightings that standard banks are required to apply have put a handbrake on competition, while larger banks with advance bank status are able to set their own risk weightings.

The two-tiered risk weighting system has often been criticised by executives at challenger banks, including ME CEO Jamie McPhee and Bendigo Bank managing director Marnie Baker, as stifling competition.

Second-tier banks were also mixed, with BoQ up 0.1 per cent, Bendigo Bank up 0.7 per cent and Suncorp down 1.5 per cent.

APRA will also make changes related to executive pay by updating its existing remuneration guidelines.

Bank royal commissioner Kenneth Hayne recommended in his final report that a cap be placed on the proportion of financial metrics used to determine long-term incentives such as shares and cash bonuses.

At a speech in April, APRA chairman Wayne Byres suggested that setting a cap at 50 per cent was a good place to start the discussion. Executive pay at the big banks has been a contentious topic over the past several years as executives collected multimillion-dollar bonuses as the banks careened from one scandal to the next.

Outrage over the practice boiled over in 2017 when CBA achieved a first strike on its remuneration proposal after the bank agreed to a $700 million payout over the AUSTRAC debacle, and in 2018 when NAB attracted a record no vote on the back of its horrendous year at the royal commission.

Under guidelines in place since 2016, large banks are required to apply a risk weighting of 25 per cent to residential mortgages while smaller banks are required to apply a risk weighting of 35 per cent.

In March 2018, the prudential regulator released a discussion paper titled "Revisions to the capital framework for authorised deposit taking institutions", which proposed banks introduce a sliding scale for risk weightings depending on the type of loan and the loan-to-valuation (LVR) ratio.

It was suggested smaller banks apply a sliding scale of risk weightings to mortgages giving them relief on loans exhibiting lower LVRs.

The paper suggested principal-and-interest loans taken out by owner-occupiers with LVRs of between 50 per cent and 80 per cent attract a risk weighting of between 20 per cent and 30 per cent.

Other residential mortgages such as those taken out by investors or interest-only loans with the same LVR would attract a weighting of between 30 per cent and 45 per cent

The risk weightings for principal-and-interest loans taken out by owner-occupiers with LVRs of between 90 per cent and 100 per cent would attract risk weightings of between 40 per cent and 50 per cent.

Other residential mortgages with the same LVRs would attract a risk weighting of between 60 and 75 per cent.

It's a small institute, and Meeuwig has been a co-author of all four of the academic publications listed on Forrest's PhD profile.

So, did Twiggy Forest spot an investment idea from his PhD in saving the oceans? Wouldn't put it past him!

But he has other links to Buru as well: the investment was made through his private company Squadron Energy, which through a joint venture is exploring in tenements adjacent to those Buru is already producing from in the Canning Basin.

It's a small world.

Curtains for Vanda Gould's $383 tax panto

It will come as a shock to readers to learn that the Anglican church's favourite accountant, Vanda Gould, has been defrocked, over the trifling matter of a $383 million tax fraud.

Yes, it seems way harsh, but the Tax Practitioners Board is firm: no more tax returns from Vanda, merely because of some findings of "sustained, calculated and layered dishonesty" made by Justice Nye Perram.

Actually Perram said a bit more in his 2014 Hua Wang Bank judgment about Gould's offshore operations. He slipped in the phrase "crooked pantomime". Oh yes.

And he directed his findings be forwarded to ASIC, the Director of Public Prosecutions and the Australian Federal Police to consider "disgraceful" conduct, money laundering, tax fraud, and possibly insider trading.

That was almost five years ago. It's only now that the TPB has decided that Vanda has delighted Tax Office auditors long enough.

The TPB's new chief exec, Michael O'Neill, will be familiar with Gould's work because as assistant tax commissioner, O'Neill headed the mammoth Project Wickenby investigation. It was Wickenby's Operation Rubix that targeted Gould and clients, including former Sunland Group chairman John Leaver and colourful investor Joe Ross.

Gould, who donated millions to the Sydney Anglican church, had his clients send money to Hua Wang Bank in Samoa (which Gould secretly owned). The "bank" sent the money back as a loan to the clients, who claimed interest payments as a tax deduction, TPB affidavits said.

It was all a fine point of law, Gould's barrister John Hyde Page told the Administrative Appeals Tribunal last week, with the winsome appeal of a man who is never sure which end of a hobby horse he most resembles.

Yes, Hyde Page said of Gould, "he did control Hua Wang Bank, his clients did deposit money, Hua Wang Bank did make loans to his clients".

But TPB counsel Anthony McInerney SC "didn't explain why that's a bad thing", Hyde Page argued. "Tax planning is what people do."

And while tax assessments had totalled $383 million, settlements to date had raised only $63 million, with $21.9 million undisputed payments and three ongoing disputes for $18 million. This was hardly enough to take away the livelihood of a man who has been a tax agent for 40 years, was Hyde Page's gist.

AAT deputy president Ian Molloy was unconvinced and this week refused a stay on Gould's deregistration, citing Perram's findings of deceitful and dishonest conduct.

"The TPB is taking a firm approach to support honest taxpayers and their advisers by terminating those agents who fail their legal and ethical responsibilities," O'Neill said.

So far this year the TPB has deregistered 70 tax agents. New broom. Ouch.

For full disclosure, Gould once threatened to launch a private criminal prosecution of your (male) columnist. Now he's suing Tax Commissioner Chris Jordan for defamation. Why not?

Blue Sky directors put it behind them

With Blue Sky Alternative Investments in administration, the listed fund manager's directors are no longer in charge. And it seems board members past and present are keen to put the whole experience behind them.

Take John Kain, for seven years the company's chairman. In early 2018, the Adelaide corporate lawyer's eponymous firm used to note his chairmanship of Blue Sky as one of his "career highlights" on his biography, listing in some detail its growing assets under management and surging market capitalisation. By June the same year, this was reduced to a single sentence noting his chairmanship of the asset manager, and by September, it was gone entirely.

At least Kain still lists his role at Blue Sky on his LinkedIn profile. It's more than can be said for the very impressive independent directors appointed to the firm in late 2018. Many hold multiple ASX board positions dutifully listed in their online resumés. But their Blue Sky appointments don't appear to have made the cut.

Andrew Day acted as Blue Sky's executive chairman until the April 2019 appointment of a new CEO. But the most recent position on his LinkedIn is his CEO role at Hastings Fund Management that ended in 2017. John McDonald is another experienced fund manager, currently a non-executive director at Crestone (where he was previously executive chairman). Blue Sky isn't on his LinkedIn. Robert Kaye, who joined the board at the same time in December, certainly appears an active user of the service. But Blue Sky is, once again, missing. As for Cheryl Edwardes, the former WA Attorney- General, experienced ASX director and member of the Foreign Investment Review Board, she tendered her resignation from Blue Sky on May 21, the day after it went into receivership. Her five months at Blue Sky also aren't listed on LinkedIn.

In their defence, all joined well after Blue Sky's troubles began, and while presumably pocketing Blue Sky's director fees couldn't find a window in which to buy a single share between the lot of them. And who could blame them for that.

Meanwhile, Blue Sky's first meeting of creditors was over in roughly 30 minutes on Thursday. It was a quiet affair, our spies not seeing a single angry shareholder at Brisbane's Waterfront Place. Administrators Bradley Hellen and Nigel Markey of Pilot Partners say their investigations are continuing.

HEADLINE: Vassie calls for rethink on Victorian gold royalty
TEXT:
Minerals Council director Bob Vassie wants Victoria to expand exemptions to its new gold royalty and consider reducing the rate, and expressed confidence the new government in Papua New Guinea will behave rationally despite the latest political instability.

Speaking in Melbourne days after the Victorian government announced a 2.75 per cent royalty on gold production, Mr Vassie said the lesson from Queensland voters' role in the federal election was that politicians should not prioritise the needs of urban voters over those in regional areas.

"People lost sight of how regional people look at [job] opportunities for them and their kids and for infrastructure in those areas," he said, in reference to the north Queensland voters' apparent support for candidates backing Adani's Carmichael coal project.

"[Western Australia] has the royalties for regions program; there was no mention of that here [in Victoria]. We want royalties off the gold, but where is it going to go? Is it going to go into Melbourne trams and buses? They misunderstand how people think and that is what happens in politics."

Mr Vassie, chairman of the Minerals Council's gold forum and chief executive of gold miner St Barbara, identified two changes he would like to see to Victoria's royalty plan if it is introduced as planned on January 1.

"I would be looking at the actual quantum because it is reasonably hefty up front, and maybe looking at the level of the trigger, if it is to come in at all," he said. The royalty is to be "triggered" once a miner produces more than 2500 ounces of gold in a year.

Mr Vassie said the Victorian government, which expects to raise $56 million over four years through the measure, had created a royalty that would deter investment in exploration, risk the viability of marginal mines and raise funds from just one mine - a reference to Kirkland Lake Gold's Fosterville mine.

"If the government had bothered to consult they might have made a better plan and I am calling on the Victorian government to take a pause, engage, talk to people and we might get a better outcome," he told the Melbourne Mining Club on Thursday.

St Barbara does not mine in Victoria, but has its headquarters in Melbourne and is the biggest shareholder in Victorian explorer Catalyst Metals, with 14.1 per cent of the company. Mr Vassie said the new royalty would not diminish St Barbara's interest in Catalyst, but it may be "a depression on people getting into exploration and funding exploration in Victoria".

St Barbara does mine in PNG, where political instability led to Peter O'Neill resigning as prime minister on Wednesday. Mr O'Neill's replacement, former finance minister James Marape, has vowed to review major resources projects in the nation, including Exxon and Oil Search's PNG LNG.

Speaking minutes before Mr Marape's elevation, Mr Vassie expressed faith that PNG would continue to be a good place to do business.

Having rebuilt St Barbara between 2014 and 2016, Mr Vassie has spent the past two years seeking an acquisition. He delivered on that goal in early May with a $768 million offer for Canada's Atlantic Gold, which will give St Barbara control of one operating mine in Nova Scotia province and three development projects nearby. The market reaction has been lukewarm, partly because the acquisition will be partly funded through an equity raising, and partly because of the permitting and development risk inherent in buying Atlantic's undeveloped gold assets.

"I have to prove why it's a good deal," said Mr Vassie on Thursday.

The need for further permits has put the spotlight on local activist groups concerned about the project's potential to create mining and tailings storage facilities within a local watershed.

Mr Vassie will meet legislators in Canada next week, and said he was confident a large section of the community was supportive. "There is support for mining industry there and there is support for jobs as well, I don't know of any new development that doesn't have some level of resistance," he said.

Canada is generally considered a supportive jurisdiction for mining, but Citi analyst Trent Allen said permits for new mines could never be assumed as guaranteed until they were obtained.
